claims.text: A Redis sorted set is a collection of unique strings, called members, ordered by an associated score. When more than one member has the same score, they are ordered lexicographically.
Redis lists leaderboards as a use case: maintaining ordered lists of the highest scores in a massive online game.

Sorted sets are implemented with a dual-ported data structure containing both a skip list and a hash table, so adding an element is an O(log(N)) operation and asking for sorted elements needs no further work.
Calling ZADD against a member already in the set updates its score and position in O(log(N)) time, which is why Redis calls sorted sets suitable when there are tons of updates.
ZINCRBY increments the score of a member, also in O(log(N)).
ZRANK returns the index of a member ordered by ascending scores and ZREVRANK by descending scores, each in O(log(N)).
ZRANGE returns the members within a range of indexes in O(log(N)+M), where M is the number of members returned; its order is low to high, and ZREVRANGE is high to low.

recall.prompt: What two structures make up a Redis sorted set, and what does adding an element cost?

answer.text: A skip list and a hash table; adding an element is O(log(N)).

recall.prompt: How are two members with the same score ordered?
Which commands give a player's rank and the top ten, and what do they cost?

answer.text: ZREVRANK gives the index by descending score in O(log(N)); ZREVRANGE returns a range high to low in O(log(N)+M).
